title: Niger Military Regime Targets LGBTQ+ Population in 'Witch-Hunt
text:
On July 1, 2026, the Nigerien military regime intensified a crackdown on LGBTQ+ individuals, detaining dozens in what activists call a “witch-hunt,” according to The Guardian. The operation, part of broader anti-terror measures, has drawn condemnation from international human rights groups and raised concerns about the country’s legal framework. The move follows years of escalating repression under the regime, which seized power in a 2023 coup.
Why the Crackdown Matters: A Human Rights Crisis in the Sahel The Nigerien military junta, led by General Aboubacar Mahamadou, has detained at least 42 individuals identified as LGBTQ+ since mid-June 2026, according to a statement from the Nigerien Association for the Defense of Human Rights (ANDH). The arrests, conducted without warrants, target “individuals suspected of engaging in ‘immoral activities,'” a term not defined in Niger’s 2010 Penal Code. The ANDH reported that detainees were subjected to interrogations and physical abuse, though no official casualties have been confirmed.
The regime’s actions align with a broader pattern of authoritarian consolidation. Since the 2023 coup, the junta has suspended the 2010 constitution, dissolved the National Assembly, and banned opposition parties. The LGBTQ+ crackdown, however, has sparked international backlash. The European Union imposed sanctions on three senior military officials in late June 2026, citing “gross human rights violations.”
Historical Context: From Colonial Laws to Modern Repression Niger’s legal stance on LGBTQ+ rights traces back to French colonial rule, which criminalized same-sex relationships under Article 338 of the 1930 Penal Code. Post-independence, Niger retained these laws, with the 2010 Penal Code explicitly banning “homosexual acts” under Article 237. The current regime has not amended these provisions, despite calls from local activists to decriminalize homosexuality.
Human Rights Watch noted in a 2025 report that Niger has one of the most restrictive legal environments for LGBTQ+ people in West Africa. “The junta’s actions are not new but a continuation of systemic discrimination,” said Amina Diallo, a legal expert at the West African Legal Network. “This crackdown risks further isolating Niger from regional and global human rights frameworks.”
Local Impact: Fear and Displacement in Niamey In the capital, Niamey, LGBTQ+ individuals have reported increased surveillance and harassment. “We’re living in constant fear,” said a 28-year-old activist, who requested anonymity due to safety concerns. “Public spaces are now dangerous. Even friends are wary of associating with us.”
ECOWAS Decides to Use Force to Remove Military Regime in Niger The crackdown has also disrupted local NGOs. The Niamey-based group [LGBTQ+ Support Network] reported a 60% drop in aid distribution since June 2026, as volunteers face arrest risks. “Our clinics and shelters are operating under extreme secrecy,” the group’s director said in a leaked video. “We’re fighting to keep our work alive.”
International Response: Diplomatic Pressure and Legal Challenges The U.S. State Department condemned the arrests in a June 2026 statement, urging Niger to “uphold its international human rights obligations.” The African Union has also called for an investigation, though its influence in Niger remains limited. Meanwhile, the International Criminal Court (ICC) has opened a preliminary inquiry into potential crimes against humanity, according to a July 2026 press release.
Legal experts argue that the regime’s actions may violate the 1966 International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), to which Niger is a party. “The arbitrary detention of LGBTQ+ individuals constitutes a clear breach of Article 9 and 14 of the ICCPR,” said Dr. Kemi Adeyemi, a Nigerian constitutional law professor. “The international community must act decisively to hold the junta accountable.”
